messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Stop Enjoyment: give up pleasant activities, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert, a 56-year-old combat pilot, had spent decades mastering the controlled chaos of aerial warfare. He was a man who trusted his instincts, his aircraft, and the precision of his own body under extreme G-forces. That trust shattered two years ago during a routine training exercise over the desert. A catastrophic engine failure produced a deafening explosion that seemed to come from inside his own skull. The cockpit filled with acrid smoke, the plane pitched violently, and Robert felt a sudden wave of dizziness so severe he could barely read his instruments. His vision blurred, nausea surged, and he knew—with a cold certainty that still visits him at night—that he was about to die. He ejected, but the memory of that helpless, spinning disorientation, ears ringing, stomach heaving, has never left him.

In the weeks after the crash, Robert was hospitalized for minor fractures and a concussion. The doctors praised his survival, but every beeping monitor and antiseptic smell made him want to flee. Physical examinations felt like another kind of assault. He started canceling follow-ups, then refused all medical appointments outright. When his wife Sarah asked him about a persistent cough, he snapped that there was nothing wrong. He had come to believe that any doctor’s office, any ambulance siren, even the sight of a bandage could pull him back into that moment of pure vulnerability.

The crash also robbed him of the things he once loved. Robert, an avid fly fisherman and weekend golfer, gradually dropped those activities. He told himself he just wasn’t interested anymore, but the truth was that every pleasant activity felt hollow, like he was watching someone else’s life. To regain some sense of control, he began restricting his eating—only small meals at exact times, no spontaneous snacks, no foods that made him feel full or queasy. His body, he reasoned, had betrayed him once; he would not let it surprise him again.

At home, Robert lives in a state of perpetual readiness. His body feels wired, as if the crash is still happening just around the corner. When Sarah walks into a room unexpectedly, he jumps, heart slamming, fists clenching. A sudden movement from a dog or a child in the park makes him flinch as though under fire. He cannot walk through a parking lot without scanning every car, every shadow. He is certain the world is now a dangerous place—not just in combat zones, but everywhere. The beliefs that once anchored him—that he was competent, that the universe was orderly—have been destroyed. He told his wife last month, “I feel dead inside. There’s nothing left.”

At work, Robert is no longer flying. He was reassigned to a desk role after the accident, ostensibly for medical reasons, though he never finished the required physical evaluation. The office is supposed to be safe, but even the hum of a photocopier or the bang of a filing cabinet sends him into a cold sweat. His colleagues notice his reluctance to leave his cubicle, his refusal to attend unit briefings near the hangar where aircraft take off. He has started avoiding the base cafeteria entirely—the noise, the crowds, the chance of hearing a sudden clatter—and eats his bland sandwich alone at his desk.

What finally brought Robert to seek help was a morning three weeks ago when he became dizzy simply standing up from a chair. The sensation was mild, only a few seconds, but it triggered a full panic attack: racing heart, hyperventilating, the conviction that he was back in the spinning cockpit. Sarah found him on the bathroom floor, sobbing and shaking. She made an appointment at a trauma clinic, and Robert came—not because he believed it would help, but because he was terrified of his own body, and even more terrified of losing his wife. He is most afraid of being told he will never feel normal again. But beneath that, in a voice he can barely acknowledge, he hopes that someone might finally give him a way to stop the world from feeling like it is always about to explode.
